title: Microprobe fuzz suite and regression retrospective
content:
Purpose and scope

This is a working retrospective and proto-spec for the microprobe fuzzing suite we used during the Feb 2025 perf regression cycle. It documents the harness architecture, the fuzz strategies we used for kernels/scheduler/KV cache, what produced useful signals, false positives we saw, and a short triage checklist for future regressions. The goal is to capture lessons learned and produce a small, reproducible set of probes that catch the class of regressions we saw in v2.14.

High-level summary (TL;DR)
- Built a lightweight synthetic trace generator that interleaves short/long context requests, random prefix reuse, and deliberate KV-cache evictions.
- Introduced scheduler perturbations (thread preemption, artificial queue skew) to surface race/priority regressions.
- Found two classes of regressions: kernel codegen path mismatch with quantized weights (reproducible via microprobe A3), and KV-cache eviction mis-indexing under high concurrency (microprobe C1).
- The harness reduced developer iteration time: average reproduce+profile time fell from ~4h to ~25m for investigated regressions.

Architecture (what we built)
- Harness components:
  - probe-generator: small Go binary that emits synthetic traces (file format: one line per request with proto fields).
  - runner: Python orchestration that can replay traces against serving-runtime binary or stubs; supports single-node and multi-worker configs.
  - monitor: collects token-level latency, kernel selection logs, KV cache hits/evictions, scheduler queue lengths, and per-request trace ids.
  - analyzer: lightweight aggregator that diffs baseline vs candidate runs and generates per-probe deltas.
- Invocation model: runner accepts a YAML matrix describing target binary, kernel-quantum profile, number of workers, batch thresholds, and a seed for the probe-generator.

Synthetic generators and corpus design
- The generator intentionally mixes three probe classes:
  1) Prefix-churn probes: many short requests with overlapping prefixes (to exercise prefix/KV sharing and cache eviction).
  2) Long-seq probes: single long-context requests with heavy KV usage (to stress kv-cache lifetime and kv-index stability).
  3) Interleaved-mix probes: a controlled sequence alternating short/long requests and occasional out-of-band cache-flush ops.
- Important knobs: token distribution (zipfian vs uniform), sequence length histogram, concurrency window, forced-eviction frequency.
- Corpus seeding: we used a mixture of real anonymized traces (20%), hand-crafted edge-cases (30%), and fully synthetic fuzzed traces (50%). The anonymized portion came from the trace-synthesis bucket but was downsampled and scrubbed.

Fuzz strategies we found effective
- KV key collision fuzz: randomly mutate keys to force table rehash and index collisions. Found bug where eviction index pointer advanced incorrectly under collision storms.
- Timing jitter injection: randomly delay worker main loop by 0-50ms to surface scheduler races — effective for revealing double-free under fast eviction path.
- Kernel feature toggles: flip quantization/FP16 paths at runtime to exercise kernel selection logic without changing model weights. Caught kernel-codepath mismatch on certain attention sizes.
- Sequence-length boundary fuzz: generate requests at boundary lengths for tiled kernels (e.g., 512/513/768) — revealed an off-by-one in kernel tile aggregator.

Scheduler perturbations (why this helped)
- We deliberately introduced artificial queue weight skew and thread preemption to move beyond clean lab conditions. Two concrete perturbations:
  1) weight-skew: bias the scheduler to accept many small requests onto one worker to see queue saturation effects. Reproduced a regression where KV eviction raced with KV insertion.
  2) preempt-slice: instruct a worker thread to sleep for short slices to emulate noisy neighbors. Triggered a deadlock in the batching path that only appeared under jitter.

KV cache specific experiments
- Forced eviction frequency matrix: run probes with eviction frequency {0,1,10,50} evictions/sec. The bug surfaced consistently at 10+ evictions/sec with concurrency >= 16.
- Eviction size stress: evict blocks of varying size to simulate multi-key invalidations. The indexing bug only occurred when evicted block sizes exceeded the inline threshold (>= 256 bytes).
- Prefetch vs on-demand: toggled prefetching of KV entries; prefetching masked the race but produced nondeterministic latencies. Conclusion: prefetch is not a safe mitigation.

Metrics and observability we recorded
- Per-probe: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, kernel_select_counts (map of kernel_id->count), kv_hit_rate, kv_eviction_rate, gc_pause_ms, worker_queue_depth_histogram.
- Tracing: request-level spans annotated with kernel_id, kv_op_id, scheduler_queue_ts, and eviction_wave_id. This was essential to correlate a late kernel selection with earlier eviction events.

Regression triage checklist (for on-call and perf leads)
1) Reproduce with harness seed used in failing e2e run (document seed/id). If fails locally, capture flamegraphs and kernel traces.
2) Toggle scheduler perturbations off/on to check sensitivity.
3) Run kv-eviction matrix (0/1/10/50) at concurrency 1/8/32. If only fails at high concurrency, gather contention metrics and per-thread stacks.
4) Run kernel feature matrix (FP32/FP16/QUANT) for the same probe — helps isolate codegen vs data mismatch.
5) If suspect, produce a minimal repro: reduce to few requests but keep critical interleaving. Submit minimal repro gist and link JIRA.
6) If non-deterministic, enable deterministic scheduler mode (if available) or record two runs and produce diff of kernel_select_counts and kv_op sequences.

False positives and noise we observed
- Cloud noise vs harness noise: some failures were caused by ephemeral host-level GC in CI runners. We moved heavy runs to reserved CI worker with disabled host GC to reduce noise.
- Metric-drift: early versions of analyzer flagged deltas <3% as regressions; threshold was reduced to 8% to prioritize signal.
- Synthetic traces too synthetic: fully fuzzed traces produced unrealistic access patterns that triggered bugs that don't exist in production. Solution: keep a steady 20% real-trace component.

Commands and example matrix (quick start)
- Generate corpus: ./probe-generator --seed 20250210 --mix prefix:0.4,long:0.3,interleaved:0.3 --out traces/seed-20250210.tgz
- Run harness baseline: python runner.py --binary ./redwood-runtime --trace traces/seed-20250210.tgz --workers 8 --kernel-profile default --evictions 10 --tag baseline-20250210
- Run candidate: python runner.py --binary ./candidate/runtime-2.14.5 --trace traces/seed-20250210.tgz --workers 8 --kernel-profile default --evictions 10 --tag candidate-20250210
- Compare: python analyzer.py --baseline baseline-20250210 --candidate candidate-20250210 --output reports/diff-20250210.json

Sample ephemeral finding (short postmortem)
- Symptom: p95 latency regressions for small prefix churn probes under high concurrency.
- Root cause: kernel selection cache key used sequence-length only, ignoring quantization flag. Under mixed FP16/quant runs the cached kernel id mismatched actual codegen path causing slow fallback and lock contention.
- Fix: change key to include quantization bits + add an assertion in kernel-selector that verifies codegen compatibility on the first use of a cached id.
- Outcome: after fix, microprobe p99 dropped to baseline and CI runs passed for seeds 20250210 and 20250224.

Next steps (action items)
- Turn the harness into a CI job gated on nightly runs for the shallow corpus (seed rotation nightly). Owner: Rohan. Due: 2025-03-10.
- Add deterministic-scheduler toggle to runner and a mode that records and replays scheduler events for flaky cases. Owner: Marco. Due: 2025-03-17.
- Curate a set of 10 minimal repro seeds (public folder) and add to linked_artifacts for easy triage. Owner: Ava. Due: 2025-03-05.

Open questions / research items
- How aggressive should eviction fuzzing be so that we surface real bugs without burning developer hours on unrealistic storms? Proposal: keep eviction knob capped at 50/sec for high-concurrency tests only.
- Can we safely instrument kernel-selector to log a fast checksum of codegen output without significant overhead? If yes, add lightweight correctness probe to production logs.

Appendix: minimal data schema for trace lines
- format: <ts_iso>	<req_id>	<type>	<len>	<prefix_hash>	<kv_ops>	<flags>
- example: 2025-02-10T14:23:11Z	req-42	prefix_churn	32	0x4b2f	[PUT:key42,GET:key19]	FP16=true,EVICT=0

Notes to the reader
- This is a working doc; experiments are still running. If you add more probes, please annotate the seed and summary of why the probe is valuable (one-line). The harness code lives in github.com/redwood/bench-harness and the primary CI job is bench-nightly/runtimes.

End of doc.
